title: Merge Sorted Linked Lists
tagline: Zip two sorted lists into one with a dummy head — the merge step of merge sort, on pointers.

intuition.analogy: Two sorted queues of people are merging into one line. You look at the two people at the front, let the shorter one in first, and repeat. Because each queue is already sorted, you only ever compare the two fronts.
paragraphs: Merging two sorted lists is the workhorse behind merge sort, k-way merges, and many interview favourites. The logic is simple: repeatedly attach the smaller current node to the result and advance that list.
A 'dummy' head node removes annoying special cases. Instead of writing extra code to set the very first node, you start with a placeholder, append to its tail, and return dummy.next at the end.
Because you only relink existing nodes (no copies), it runs in O(1) extra space. When one list runs out, you splice the remainder of the other in a single pointer assignment.
intuition.keyIdea: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer; always append the smaller front node, then attach the leftover tail.

steps.title: Create a dummy head
steps.detail: dummy is a throwaway node; tail points at it. This avoids branching for the first element.

steps.title: Compare fronts and splice
steps.detail: While both lists are non-empty, attach the smaller head to tail.next, advance that list and tail.

steps.title: Attach the remainder
steps.detail: One list is now empty; point tail.next at whatever's left of the other. Return dummy.next.

complexity.timeReason: Each node from both lists is visited once.
complexity.spaceReason: Only pointers are rearranged; no new nodes are allocated.

pitfalls: Forgetting to attach the non-empty remainder leaves the merged list truncated.
Using '<' vs '<=' affects stability when values tie.
Returning dummy instead of dummy.next includes the placeholder node.

dryRun.clickMoment: Notice you never look past the two fronts. Sorted inputs mean the global minimum is always one of the two current heads — that's why a single comparison per step suffices.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.statement: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

approach: Use a dummy head and a tail pointer. Repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes and advance that list.
When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other. O(n+m), O(1) extra.

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.statement: Merge k sorted lists into one.
problems.hint: Pairwise merge in a tournament, or use a min-heap of k heads.

approach: Keep a min-heap of the current head of each list. Pop the smallest, append it, and push its successor.
Each of the n nodes is pushed/popped once at O(log k), giving O(n log k).

problems.title: Sort List
problems.statement: Sort a linked list in O(n log n).
problems.hint: Split with fast/slow, sort halves, merge.

approach: Top-down merge sort on the list: split at the middle (slow/fast), sort both halves, and merge.
Pointer rewiring keeps space at O(log n) recursion only; guaranteed O(n log n).

problems.title: Merge Sorted Array
problems.statement: Merge two sorted arrays in-place into the first.
problems.hint: Fill from the back to avoid overwriting unprocessed elements.

approach: Merge in place from the back so we never overwrite unmerged values of nums1. Three pointers: ends of the real data in nums1, nums2, and the write position.
Place the larger of the two tails at the write pointer and step backward. O(m+n).

problems.title: Add Two Numbers
problems.statement: Add two numbers stored as linked lists (least-significant first).
problems.hint: Walk both lists together with a carry, building the result with a dummy head.
problems.tests: Dummy-head construction while traversing two lists.

approach: Digits are stored in reverse, so we can add front-to-back like grade-school addition, carrying as we go.
Use a dummy head; at each step sum the two current digits plus carry, create a node with sum%10, carry sum/10. Continue while either list or carry remains.

codes.title: solution.cpp
solution.py
codes.source:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, a, b):
        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        carry = 0
        while a or b or carry:
            s = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
            carry = s // 10
            tail.next = ListNode(s % 10)
            tail = tail.next
            a = a.next if a else None
            b = b.next if b else None
        return dummy.next
